items.stem:
Assertion : Radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is half its focal length.
Reason : A ray of light incident parallel to principal axis after reflection passes through C.
items.assertion: Radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is half its focal length.
items.reason: A ray of light incident parallel to principal axis after reflection passes through C.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are false.

items.answer: (d) Both Assertion and Reason are false. The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is always twice the focal length, as it is the distance between the centre of curvature and the pole of the mirror, whereas the focal length is the distance between the focus and the pole. The relation between focal length (f) and radius of curvature (R) is f = R/2. A ray incident parallel to the principal axis passes through the focus F after reflection, not through C. So neither assertion nor reason is true.
items.ocr: Printed in the OBJECTIVE (Assertion-Reason) run, but MinerU placed questions 29-32 on page 16 inside the ONE MARK character range, so they are read here. Legend options relabelled (a)-(d) to A-D.

items.stem:
Assertion : After refraction through a rectangular glass slab, emergent ray is parallel to the direction of incident ray.
Reason : Refractive indices of air and glass are different.
items.assertion: After refraction through a rectangular glass slab, emergent ray is parallel to the direction of incident ray.
items.reason: Refractive indices of air and glass are different.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

options.label: D

items.answer: (b) Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion. After refraction through a rectangular glass slab the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray because the two opposite faces of the slab at which refraction takes place are parallel to each other. The refractive indices of air and glass are indeed different, but that is not the cause of the emergent ray being parallel to the incident ray. Hence both are true but the reason is not the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Assertion : Magnification of real images is taken negative.
Reason : Magnification is ratio of image distance and object distance.
items.assertion: Magnification of real images is taken negative.
items.reason: Magnification is ratio of image distance and object distance.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are false.

items.answer: (c) Assertion is true but Reason is false. Magnification of a real image is taken negative. The height of the object is taken positive as the object is usually placed above the principal axis, while a real image is always inverted so its height is taken negative; magnification is the ratio of image height to object height, so it comes out negative. Magnification is the ratio of image height to object height, m = h₂/h₁, and is related to the distances as m = −v/u, so the reason as stated is false.
items.ocr: Legend options relabelled (a)-(d) to A-D. Question sits on page 16, inside the ONE MARK character range.

items.stem:
Assertion : On moving from optically rarer to denser medium, a ray of light bends away from the normal.
Reason : Speed of light is more in denser medium and less in rarer medium.
items.assertion: On moving from optically rarer to denser medium, a ray of light bends away from the normal.
items.reason: Speed of light is more in denser medium and less in rarer medium.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion is true but Reason is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion and Reason are false.

items.answer: (d) Both Assertion and Reason are false. When a light ray travels from an optically rarer to an optically denser medium it bends towards the normal, not away from it. Also the speed of light is less in a denser medium and more in a rarer medium. Hence neither the assertion nor the reason is true.

items.stem: What is light ?
items.answer: Light is the form of energy which gives sensation of vision.

items.stem: What kind of wave is light ?
items.answer: Light is an electromagnetic wave.

items.stem: What is image ?
items.answer: Image of an object is formed when reflected or refracted rays intersect each other.

items.stem: What is real image ?
items.answer: Real image is formed by real intersection of refracted or reflected rays.

items.stem: What is virtual image ?
items.answer: Virtual image is formed by the virtual intersection of refracted or reflected rays.

items.stem: For regular reflection what is relation between angle of incidence and angle of reflection ?
items.answer: Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection.

items.stem: When a ray is made incident normal to the plane, what is angle of incidence and angle of reflection ?
items.answer: The angle of incidence and angle of reflection both are of zero degree (0°).

items.stem: Write the mirror formula.
items.answer: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, where v is the image distance, u the object distance and f the focal length of the mirror.
items.ocr: MinerU's column order printed this answer's display formula further down the page (after question 58's stem); reattached to question 50 by its wording.

items.stem: Write the formula of magnification.
items.answer: m = h₂/h₁ = −v/u, where h₂ is the height of the image, h₁ the height of the object, v the image distance and u the object distance.
items.ocr: Answer formula recovered from the display block that MinerU emitted after the stem; LaTeX rewritten to Unicode.

items.stem: Write one use of concave and convex mirrors each.
items.answer: Concave mirror is used in solar concentration, while convex mirror is used as rear view mirror in automobiles.

items.stem: Why do we use convex mirror for side-view mirror ?
items.answer: Convex mirror is used for side view because it forms a virtual, erect and smaller (diminished) image, which gives a large field of view.
items.ocr: Stray 'Ans b' marker after the stem dropped; printed answer read 'virtual, erect and image smaller' - word order repaired to 'erect and smaller image'.

items.stem: Can a virtual image be screened ?
items.answer: No, virtual image cannot be screened.

items.stem: Define the focus of a spherical mirror.
items.answer: The virtual or real point on the principal axis where all the light rays parallel to the principal axis meet after reflection is called the principal focus.

items.stem: What is centre of curvature of convex mirror ?
items.answer: The convex mirror is a part of a hollow sphere having its inward surface polished. The inside centre of that sphere is called the centre of curvature of the convex mirror.

items.stem: What is the minimum distance between an object and its real image in case of a concave mirror ?
items.answer: Zero (the object and its real image coincide at the centre of curvature).
items.ocr: The same question is printed again as number 89 (Foreign 2010) later in this section; both printed copies are kept.

items.stem: Draw a ray diagram to show reflection of an incident ray parallel to principal axis by a convex mirror.
items.answer: A ray travelling parallel to the principal axis of a convex mirror is reflected such that the reflected ray appears to diverge from the principal focus F lying behind the mirror. In the ray diagram the incident ray is drawn parallel to the principal axis up to the reflecting surface and the reflected ray is drawn diverging away from the axis, with its backward extension (dotted) passing through F, which lies between the pole P and the centre of curvature C behind the mirror.
items.ocr: The printed answer is a figure only; MinerU captured no image for page 15 (its leftovers 'F' and 'C' are the figure's labels), so the diagram is described in words and no image is attached.

items.stem: If the object is placed between the pole P and focus F of the concave mirror, what will be the position, size and nature of the image formed ?
items.answer: The image formed is virtual, enlarged, erect and lies behind the mirror.

items.stem: What is value of speed of light in vacuum ?
Does the speed of light change with medium ?
items.answer: Yes, speed of light changes with medium.

items.stem:
(a) Draw a ray diagram to show the refraction of light through a glass slab and mark angle of refraction and lateral shift suffered by the ray of light passing through the slab.
(b) If the refractive index of glass for light going from air to glass is 3/2, find the refractive index of air for light going from glass to air.
items.answer:
(a) In the ray diagram the incident ray strikes the first face of the rectangular glass slab and bends towards the normal; inside the slab it travels as the refracted ray making the angle of refraction r with the normal, and at the second face it bends away from the normal and emerges parallel to the original incident ray. The perpendicular distance between the direction of the incident ray produced and the emergent ray is the lateral shift (lateral displacement).
(b) n(air → glass) = 3/2 = 1.5, therefore n(glass → air) = 1 / n(air → glass) = 1/1.5 = 2/3 ≈ 0.67.
items.ocr: Printed number 77 places this in the ONE MARK run (43-89), so marks kept at 1 even though it carries two parts. LaTeX fractions rewritten to Unicode. The figure on page 17 belongs to the worked solution, so no image is attached.

items.stem: A ray of light is incident on a convex mirror as shown. Redraw the diagram and complete the path of this ray after reflection from the mirror. Mark angle of incidence and angle of reflection on it.
items.answer: Draw the normal at the point of incidence by joining that point to the centre of curvature C, which lies behind the convex mirror. The reflected ray is then drawn on the other side of this normal so that the angle of reflection ∠r equals the angle of incidence ∠i (∠i = ∠r), and it therefore diverges away from the principal axis.
items.ocr: Two figures sit next to this question on page 17: the first (attached) is the printed question diagram, the second is the answer diagram and is deliberately not attached. The printed solution is a figure only, so the answer is described in words.

items.stem: Define the term principal focus for a convex mirror.
items.answer: It is the point on the principal axis of a convex mirror from where the rays of light, which are incident parallel to the principal axis, appear to come after reflection.
items.ocr: Printed answer is garbled ('at which the rays parallel to the principle axis from where the rays of light seem to come after reflection'); rewritten as one grammatical sentence without changing its meaning.

items.stem: What are the units of power of a lens ?
items.answer: Dioptre (D).

items.stem: In what condition, the image formed by a concave mirror is virtual ?
items.answer: When the object is placed between the focus and the pole of a concave mirror, a virtual image is obtained.

items.stem: Name the type of mirror which always forms a virtual and diminished image.
items.answer: Convex mirror.

items.stem: Name the type of mirror which is known as shaving mirror.
items.answer: Concave mirror. Concave mirrors are used as shaving mirrors because they magnify the image.

items.stem: How does the size of the image change as the object is brought closer from infinity towards the convex lens ?
items.answer: The size of the image formed keeps on increasing as the object is brought closer towards the convex lens.
items.ocr: Missing question mark at the end of the printed stem restored.

items.stem: The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. What is the meaning of this statement ?
items.answer: The refractive index of diamond being 2.42 means that the speed of light in diamond is reduced by a factor of 2.42 as compared to its speed in air.

items.stem: The power of a lens is −4.0 D. What is the nature of the lens ?
items.answer: The lens is a diverging (concave) lens, because its power and hence its focal length is negative.
items.ocr: Printed question number was lost by MinerU; inferred as 86 from its position between questions 85 and 87. LaTeX '$-4.0$ D' rewritten as −4.0 D.

items.stem: Define refractive index of a medium.
items.answer: Refractive index of a medium, n = Speed of light in vacuum (c) / Speed of light in given medium (v).
items.ocr: Spaced-out LaTeX of the definition ('S p e e d ~ o f ~ l i g h t ...') rejoined into readable text.

items.stem: Refractive index of water with respect to air is 1.33. What is the refractive index of air with respect to water ?
items.answer: n(air w.r.t. water) = 1 / n(water w.r.t. air) = 1/1.33 = 0.75
items.ocr: LaTeX subscripted symbols n_aw and n_wa written out as n(air w.r.t. water) and n(water w.r.t. air).

items.stem: What is the minimum distance between an object and its real image in case of a concave mirror ?
items.answer: Zero (the object and its real image coincide when the object is at the centre of curvature).

items.stem: How do we distinguish a medium to be rarer or denser ?
items.answer: We distinguish a medium to be denser or rarer on the basis of the following facts : (i) A denser medium has a higher value of refractive index. (ii) When a light ray travels from a rarer to a denser medium it bends towards the normal, and vice-versa.

items.stem: State Snell's Law.
items.answer: The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant, for a given colour and for the given pair of media: sin i / sin r = μ (constant).
items.ocr: Numbered 98, so printed in the TWO MARKS run; read here because MinerU placed page 19 inside the ONE MARK character range. LaTeX formula rewritten to Unicode.

items.stem: What is the meaning of (i) optical centre and (ii) principal axis ?
items.answer: (i) Optical centre : It is the point of a lens through which a light ray passes without deviation. (ii) Principal axis : The line joining the optical centre and the focus of the lens is called the principal axis.
items.ocr: Numbered 99, so printed in the TWO MARKS run; read here because MinerU placed page 19 inside the ONE MARK character range.

items.stem: When does a convex lens form (i) a virtual, erect, enlarged image (ii) real, enlarged image ?
items.answer: (i) For a virtual, erect and enlarged image the object is placed between the optical centre and the focus in front of a convex lens. (ii) For a real and enlarged image the object is kept between F and 2F in front of a convex lens.
items.ocr: Printed answer shows F as "F'" (stray prime from the LaTeX); read as F. Numbered 100, so printed in the TWO MARKS run and read here from page 19.

items.stem: State laws of refraction of light.
items.answer: The following are the laws of refraction of light: (i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface of two transparent media at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. (ii) The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant, for light of a given colour and for the given pair of media - this is Snell's law of refraction: sin i / sin r = constant. This constant value is called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
items.ocr: LaTeX formula rewritten to Unicode. Numbered 101, so printed in the TWO MARKS run and read here from page 19.

items.stem:
(a) What happens to a ray of light when it travels from one medium to another having equal refractive indices ?
(b) State the cause of refraction of light.
items.answer: (a) No refraction or bending would take place; the light will travel in a straight line. (b) Refraction occurs due to the change in the speed of light as it enters from one medium into another.
items.ocr: Numbered 102, so printed in the TWO MARKS run and read here from page 19.

items.stem: What is meant by refractive index ? If the speed of light in a medium is 2/3 rd of the speed of light in vacuum, find the refractive index of that medium.
items.answer: Refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium. R.I. = c/v = c / ((2/3) of c) = 1.5
items.ocr: LaTeX fraction rewritten to Unicode text. Numbered 103, so printed in the TWO MARKS run and read here from page 19.

items.stem: One portion of a convex lens is covered as shown. Will the lens produce a complete image of the object ? Describe in brief the characteristics of the image formed.
items.answer: Yes, the lens would produce a complete image. The image will be complete but with reduced intensity, i.e. the image formed will be fainter (blurred).

items.stem: The given diagram shows an object O and its image I. Copy the diagram in your answer book and draw suitable rays to locate the lens and its focus. Name the type of lens in this case.
items.answer: Join the top of the object O to the top of its image I; this ray passes undeviated through the optical centre, and where it cuts the principal axis fixes the position of the lens. Then draw a ray from the top of O parallel to the principal axis; after refraction it passes through (or appears to come from) the focus, which locates F. For the diagram printed with this question the image is erect and diminished and lies on the same side as the object, so the lens used is a concave lens.

items.stem:
(a) A ray of light starting from diamond is incident on the interface separating diamond and water. Draw a labelled ray diagram to show the refraction of light in this case.
(b) Absolute refractive indices of diamond and water are 2.42 and 1.33 respectively. Find the value of refractive index of water w.r.t. diamond.
items.answer:
(a) The labelled ray diagram shows the ray travelling in diamond striking the diamond-water interface, the normal drawn at the point of incidence, and the refracted ray in water bending away from the normal, since water is optically rarer than diamond.
(b) Given, refractive index of diamond = 2.42 and refractive index of water = 1.33. Refractive index of water with respect to diamond = 1.33 / 2.42 = 0.55

items.stem:
A concave mirror is used for image formation for different positions of an object. What inferences can be drawn about the following when an object is placed at a distance of 10 cm from the pole of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm ?
(a) Position of the image
(b) Size of the image
(c) Nature of the image
Draw a labelled ray diagram to justify your inferences.
items.answer:
Object distance, u = −10 cm; focal length of the concave mirror, f = −15 cm. From the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = (−1/15) − (−1/10) = (−2 + 3)/30 = 1/30, so v = +30 cm.
(a) Position: the image is formed 30 cm behind the mirror (on the same side as the object's side of viewing, i.e. it is not in front of the mirror).
(b) Size: magnification m = −v/u = −(+30)/(−10) = +3, so the image is three times the size of the object, i.e. enlarged.
(c) Nature: since v is positive and m is positive, the image is virtual and erect. The ray diagram is drawn with the object between the pole P and the focus F, one incident ray parallel to the principal axis reflecting through F and another directed towards C reflecting back along itself; the backward extensions of the reflected rays meet behind the mirror to give the virtual, erect and enlarged image.
